messages.subject: 95% credible intervals for annual occupancy estimates
messages.subject_clean: 95% credible intervals for annual occupancy estimates
messages.body_plain:
I feel like this should be an easy problem to solve but can't figure it out for some reason. I am trying to obtain 95% credible intervals around each year's estimated psi value when using the tPGOcc model. For example, I get the annual average psi of model (out) using:

psi.avg<-apply(out$psi.samples,3,mean)

To get the credible intervals I thought it should be something like:

psi.CRI<-apply(out$psi.samples,3,function(x){quantile(x,probs=c(0.025,0.975))})

However, this gives me intervals that span basically 0-1 in most years which didn't seem right. My model showed convergence based on rhat and had okay Bayesian p-value (0.16) so I wouldn't have thought the CRIs would have been that wide but maybe I'm missing obvious here. Any thoughts either confirming I did this incorrectly, or that it is correct and that I should investigate the model fit further would be greatly appreciated.

Tom

messages.subject: Re: 95% credible intervals for annual occupancy estimates
messages.subject_clean: 95% credible intervals for annual occupancy estimates
messages.body_plain:
Hi Tom,

Based on what you described, it sounds to me like you want to determine the average occupancy probability across all your sites in each year, and then get a credible interval around that average. To get the means, the approach you used is just fine, but the credible intervals need to be calculated in a slightly different way. You should first calculate (for each MCMC iteration), the average occupancy probability across all sites in each year. Then you can use that to get the 95% credible interval for "average occupancy probability in each year". Here's some code that should allow you to do that, and explore how the two approaches give different values for the credible intervals. So, the thing I call "psi.mean.quants" below is what I think you want.

# Posterior samples of the average occupancy across all sites within each year
psi.mean.samples <- apply(out$psi.samples, c(1, 3), mean)
psi.means <- apply(out$psi.samples, 3, mean)
psi.mean.of.means <- apply(psi.mean.samples, 2, mean)
# psi.means and psi.mean.of.means will be the same
all.equal(psi.means, psi.mean.of.means)
# However, the same is not true for the quantiles
psi.quants <- apply(out$psi.samples, 3, quantile, c(0.025, 0.975))
psi.mean.quants <- apply(psi.mean.samples, 2, quantile, c(0.025, 0.975))
psi.quants
psi.mean.quants

Jeff

messages.subject: spPGOcc Error
messages.body_plain:
Hello,

Thank you for creating these packages and setting up this platform for questions. I have a query regarding spOccupancy.

I am attempting to do a nationwide occupancy assessment of a rare species. I have camera trap data from ~1500 camera traps from nine sites across Uganda, therefore the survey design is clustered with distance between all cameras ranging from <20m to >500,000km. The detection history is up to 36 5-day sampling occasions (~6 months) for each camera.

To fully explore my data, and as this is my first time using the package (and Bayesian stats!), I have done a number of exploratory steps to help my understanding. Firstly, I ran occupancy models using unmarked to see whether the models would converge with all my variables and explore which variables were most influential. I then ran the  ‘PGOcc’ function on the null, global and best resulting model from unmarked – these all ran without any issues using the defaults from the article here: Introduction to spOccupancy • spOccupancy <https://doserlab.com/files/spoccupancy-web/articles/modelfitting#spPGOcc>

However, the reason for wanting to use this package was to explore and account for any issues with spatial correlation.  I used the ‘spPGOcc’ function on the full dataset (not taking into account the clustered sample design) on the null, global and best models, again using the default values from the blog above. The models ran but my rhat values were incredibly large. For example, here is the summary output from my global model:

After reading this blog,

Convergence diagnostics and other considerations when fitting spatial occupancy models • spOccupancy <https://doserlab.com/files/spoccupancy-web/articles/modelconsiderations#specifying-the-prior-for-the-spatial-decay-parameter-phi-in-spatial-occupancy-models>

 and the paper by Bajcz et al. (2024) I have tried to use more informed priors, using minimum and maximum distances between cameras within each study site rather than the whole country, which ranges from ~ 20m – 40km. I used the equation in Bajcz et al to calculate X and W, but have left all other remaining values the same, as so:

informed.priors <- list(beta.normal = list(mean = 0, var = 2.72),

                    alpha.normal = list(mean = 0, var = 2.72),

                    sigma.sq.ig = c(2, 1),

                    phi.unif = c(3/(40754/2), 1/1903))

However, when I try to run any models, they fail to run, and I get the following error message:

Error in spPGOcc(occ.formula = null.formula, det.formula = null.formula,  : c++ error: dpotrf failed

I have checked for duplicated coordinates but there aren’t any. Does anyone have any suggestions on what might be going wrong?

Any guidance would be greatly appreciated.

Best wishes,

Naomi

messages.subject: Re: spPGOcc Error
messages.body_plain:
Hi Naomi,

My first guess as to why you're getting that error is because you may have an invalid initial value for phi. If you were using the initial values described in the vignette and did not change the initial value for phi after specifying a more informative prior, then it is likely outside the range of the uniform prior that is specified on phi and will result in an immediate error like the one you have there. You could either specify the initial value for phi to make sure it is within the bounds of the new uniform distribution you are specifying in "phi.unif", or you could just take the initial value for phi out of the "spat.inits" list completely, in which case the function will by default choose a good initial value for you. Once you do that I'm guessing the error should go away.

Additionally, I noticed you are running the model for 10,000 samples per chain, which is not all that much for a spatial occupancy model, particularly when you have a lot of sites. While 10,000 iterations in the vignette resulted in a model that converged (or was very close to converging), that may not be the case for other data sets, particularly one like yours where you have substantially more sites than what I used in the vignette. So, you may need to run the model for 50,000 iterations or even 100,000 iterations (or potentially more).

Let me know if I can clarify anything,

Jeff

messages.subject: msDS in spAbundance with multiple visits.
messages.subject_clean: msDS in spAbundance with multiple visits.
messages.body_plain:
Hi,
This is perhaps a basic question, but I am attempting to run a multi-species distance sampling model in SpAbundance.

I have count data for 5 salamander species along a number of 25 x 4m transects. Each transect had repeated visits.

Is it possible to incorporate the data of repeated visits? The example vignette seems to be over a single visit. When using spOccupancy vignette to package the data to the correct format, "K" corresponds to maximum number of visits and "det.covs" allows for the covariates recorded at each visit. Yet when I attempt to us msDS in spAbundance "K" corresponds to the distance breaks of the searches and "covs" is not broken up into detection and abundance covariates which seems to disallow repeated visits.

Is there a way to format the data for repeated visits into msDS or does it only work on  single visit data sets?

Thanks,
Zac

Sorry about that!

Jeff

messages.subject: Re: msDS in spAbundance with multiple visits.
messages.subject_clean: msDS in spAbundance with multiple visits.
messages.body_plain:
Ah, thanks, Marc, yes I was thinking solely in terms of spatial models.

For the simplest non-spatial distance sampling models (so DS and msDS, and also NMix and msNMix for the n-mixture models), if you organize the data in a "stacked" manner than you can fit a basic multi-visit design, but note that this is different from the "repeated visits" of an N-mixture model in the sense that density is allowed to change across the visits.  Following the verbiage used in spOccupancy, this would be a basic "multi-season" distance sampling model. So, the rows of the "y" matrix would be "site-visits" instead of just "sites", the columns would still be the distance bands, and the "covs" would be the same length as "site-visits", which would allow you to include variation spatially and temporally across sites and the multiple visits. You could then include certain random effects to do some basic accounting of pseudoreplication as Marc points out.

Jeff

Following the verbiage used in spOccupancy, this would be a basic "multi-season" distance sampling model. So, the rows of the "y" matrix would be "site-visits" instead of just "sites", the columns would still be the distance bands, and the "covs" would be the same length as "site-visits", which would allow you to include variation spatially and temporally across sites and the multiple visits. messages.subject: spOccupancy v0.8.0 now on CRAN
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

spOccupancy v0.8.0 is now on CRAN. This version contains some new functionality that may be of interest, particularly in the context of integrated models:
Three new functions for fitting multi-season single-species integrated occupancy models: tIntPGOcc (nonspatial), stIntPGOcc (spatial), and svcTIntPGOcc (spatially-varying coefficients).
All single-species integrated models now support occupancy and detection random intercepts using lme4 syntax. This allows you to include different detection random effects for different data sources.
Some new GoF functionality for basic single-species occupancy models (functions PGOcc, spPGOcc, svcPGOcc). This allows for calculation of occupancy and detection residuals following the approach of Wilson et al. (2019). If you use this and find it useful, then please let me know as that will help me determine if I should implement for other model types.
Cheers,

Jeff

messages.subject: Re: spPGOcc Error
messages.body_plain:
Hi Naomi,

Gerat, glad to hear that you've got the models to run. Yes, you should try and ensure that phi is converged and less than 1.1 as well, although this (and sigma.sq) are notoriously difficult parameters to get to converge so it may be more difficult to achieve than for the other parameters. First, I would suggest looking at the traceplots for the spatial covariance parameters, which you can do with plot(out, 'theta', density = FALSE), where you replace the name of "out" with whatever you saved your output from spPGOcc as. This will give you more of an indication of the convergence of phi as opposed to just the Rhat value. You also will likely want to increase the burn-in to something larger than 2000, perhaps to something like 40,000. That may remove some parts of the sample towards the beginning of the model run that have not reached convergence (which you may see in the traceplot).

Jeff

messages.subject: Larger uncertainty in multiseason model vs single season + mirrored detection probabilities
messages.subject_clean: Larger uncertainty in multiseason model vs single season + mirrored detection probabilities
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

I have been running the same data through single and multi season data using non-spatial single species occupancy models (PGOcc and tPGocc). I have approximately 40 sites of data (varies a little depending on the season) and 4 seasons (Spring and Summer 2023 and 2024; each with three 1-month replicate surveys). I tested various different occurrence and detection covariate combinations for each time period to find the models with the lowest WAIC and K-fold deviation scores (along with acceptable Bayesian P values).

I have attached 4 screenshots; 2 showing the single and multiseason model occupancy and detection probability estimates (text labels = SD). The multiseason model is the one where occupancy estimates for each season are much flatter, with an SD of 0.46. The other 2 plots compare the occupancy and detection probabilities, respectively, of the single and multiseason models for easier visualisation.

As the multi-season model considers all of the data together, I would have imagined it to have a larger sample size and thus less uncertainty in the data, reflected in a smaller standard deviation compared with the single season estimates, but instead it is the opposite! Does anyone know why this might be the case? And why the multiseason occupancy probability estimates would be so flat/consistent between the seasons? I have heard that as the multiseason models consider occupancy/ detection/nondetection in neighbouring seasons, it can 'bring up' the values in seasons where single-season models estimate lower occupancy.

In a different site, my multiseason model estimates were not this flat/consistent and showed greater variability (although those models included autumn and winter data while these just include spring/summer as there were generally 0 detections in these seasons for this site).

I am still trying to make sense of this and am not sure how to explain it in my reports. Any help is much appreciated!

I'm also wondering how to explain how in the plot showing estimated detection probabilities for single and multiseason models, when the single season model predicts higher probabilities, the multi season predicts lower, and vice versa. Why don't they follow the same trend?

If anyone needs any more information to help, please don't hesitate to ask!

Cheers!

Merry Christmas and a Happy New Year!
Jamie
